newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds firmer as market volumes thin.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds firmer as market volumes thin.

text.p: Irish bonds were firmer in quiet afternoon trade on Thursday with longer yield paper further recouping some of the losses triggered by a large-scale sell-off of the Irish pound on Wednesday, dealers said.

"Really the bond market has held up remarkably well despite the tighter money market," a dealer said. "We've seen curve-flattening and the short end has been most affected - particularly the two-year bond - but at the long end it's not bad."
By 1515 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 was up four pence to 101.89 to yield 5.99 percent, having fallen 50 pence from Tuesday's close to 101.45 to yield 6.11 by midday Wednesday.

The key benchmark eight percent bond due 2006 was up 38 pence at 108.98 to yield 6.66 percent having fallen 43 pence from the close to 108.10 to yield 6.79 percent during the early session on Wednesday.
Dealers said Irish bonds were yielding 152 basis points over German bunds in the five-year area, and 87 basis points over Germany in the 10-year area, a convergence to bunds of five basis points.
The worst-hit two-year bond was up seven basis points from Wednesday's close.

The fall-off in trade later in the session was due to the market's focus being distracted by Britain's poll and the lack of business from key European markets, closed for a May Day holiday, dealers said.
The rate of the Irish pound's descent was also slowed by thin volumes in the market, although selling interest remains and the unit is expected to continue its slide.

The Irish pound hit a five-year low against sterling on Wednesday and dropped 6.5 pfennigs against the mark after Ireland's central bank indicated it was not going to intervene to shore up the ailing currency.

The punt encountered huge selling pressure on the assumption that Ireland would have to drop to the central rate within the European Exchange Rate Mechanism if it hopes to enter a single currency in 1999. This would imply a level of 2.41 against the mark, dealers said.

Ireland's Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn on Wednesday tried to soothe markets, saying Ireland did not necessarily have to enter a single currency at the central rate. He said no decision had been made on this yet.
Economists said on Thursday they expected the mark/punt to find a floor at around 2.53 marks, by which stage the forward rates would be discounting a move back to its ERM central parity.
"What we need is for sterling to fall by between five and ten pfennigs, which would ease speculation on the punt," a dealer said.
